definition: A subtle difference in meaning, tone, feeling or colour.

examples.text: My tutor said the essay was strong but missed some of the nuance in Orwell's argument.
There's a nuance here: 'weight' and 'mass' aren't the same thing, even though we use them interchangeably at home.
The spec captures the main flow, but there's nuance around how refunds interact with partial orders.
There's a nuance between being frugal and being stingy.

synonyms.note: Broader; can describe skill or tact as well as meaning.
More literary; used almost only about language.

commonMistake: The adjective is 'nuanced' (a nuanced view), not 'nuanceful'.
origin: From French 'nuer', to shade, from 'nue', cloud: think of the shifting shades in a cloud.

upgrade.plain: There's a small difference between the two options that matters.
upgrade.model: There's an important nuance that separates the two options.

definition: Expressed clearly in few words.

examples.text: Keep your abstract succinct: 150 words, and every sentence should earn its place.
Can someone give me a succinct definition of photosynthesis, in one sentence?
Her PR descriptions are always succinct: what changed, why, and how to test it.
Keep the birthday card message succinct; there isn't much room.

synonyms.note: Very close; 'concise' stresses brevity, 'succinct' stresses clarity and precision too.
Short to the point of sounding curt or unfriendly.
Short and clever or memorable, e.g. a pithy remark.

commonMistake: Pronounced 'suk-SINKT', with a hard 'k' sound; not 'suss-INKT'.
origin: Latin 'succinctus', girded up: clothing tucked in tightly so nothing hangs loose.

upgrade.plain: Your report was short and clear.
upgrade.model: Your report was admirably succinct.

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.

examples.text: Rather than rewriting the whole dissertation, we agreed on a pragmatic fix to the literature review.
It's a pragmatic choice: we'll use the calculator method now and revisit the proof next term.
Let's be pragmatic and ship the simple version; we can optimise once we have real usage data.
We took a pragmatic approach and ordered pizza.

synonyms.note: More general; 'pragmatic' implies a deliberate trade-off against an ideal.
Focuses on what is achievable rather than on method.

origin: Greek 'pragma', a deed or act: concerned with doing rather than theorising.

upgrade.plain: We should be sensible and do the simple thing first.
upgrade.model: We should take a pragmatic approach and do the simple thing first.

definition: A warning or condition that limits what has just been said.

examples.text: The results look promising, with the caveat that the sample was only 30 people.
One caveat: this rule only works for right-angled triangles.
It's ready to release, with one caveat: the export feature hasn't been tested on Safari.
I'll come to the party, with one caveat: I'm leaving by ten.

synonyms.note: More formal; a condition attached to an agreement.
A statement that limits a claim; common in academic writing.

origin: Latin for 'let him beware', as in 'caveat emptor': let the buyer beware.

upgrade.plain: It works, but there's one thing to be careful about.
upgrade.model: It works, with one caveat.

definition: Not revealing your thoughts or feelings readily; reserved.

examples.text: He's quite reticent in seminars, but his written work is outstanding.
Some reticent pupils will answer happily on a mini whiteboard but never put their hand up.
The client was reticent about their budget, which made scoping the project tricky.
My grandad is reticent about his time in the army.

synonyms.note: Unwilling to do something; 'reticent' is about not speaking or revealing.

commonMistake: Careful usage keeps 'reticent' for 'not saying much', not simply 'reluctant' ('reluctant to sign', not 'reticent to sign').
origin: Latin 'reticere', to keep silent.

upgrade.plain: She didn't say much about why she left.
upgrade.model: She was reticent about why she left.

definition: Truthful and straightforward, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

examples.text: Can I be candid? I don't think the conclusion follows from your data.
I had a candid conversation with his parents about his attendance.
Retros only work if people feel safe enough to be candid.
Can I be candid? That haircut isn't your best.

synonyms.note: Very close; 'frank' can sound slightly blunter.
Direct without softening; often implies a lack of tact.
Willing to share; less about saying difficult things.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of a photo: taken without the subject posing, or knowing.
otherMeanings.example: The best wedding photos were the candid ones.

origin: Latin 'candidus', white or pure. A Roman 'candidatus' wore a white toga.

upgrade.plain: To be honest, I'm not sure this will work.
upgrade.model: To be candid, I'm not convinced this will work.

definition: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise.

examples.text: Her referencing is meticulous: not a single missing page number.
Your lab notes are meticulous; anyone could repeat this experiment from them.
He's meticulous in code review and often spots edge cases the tests miss.
She's meticulous about planning holidays, right down to the last train.

synonyms.note: Complete, covering everything; less focus on precision.
Stresses the effort and time involved.
Negative: overly concerned with minor details or rules.

origin: Latin 'meticulosus', fearful: originally someone so afraid of mistakes they checked everything.

upgrade.plain: She checks every detail very carefully.
upgrade.model: She is meticulous about every detail.

definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something.

examples.text: I'm ambivalent about the group project: I like the topic but not the deadline.
Staff are ambivalent about the new homework policy; it saves marking but pupils do less practice.
I'm ambivalent about the rewrite: it would fix the tech debt, but it'll freeze features for a quarter.
I'm ambivalent about moving to the countryside.

synonyms.note: Informal British equivalent: 'I'm in two minds about it.'
Stronger emotional pull in two directions.
Not the same: no strong feelings at all.

commonMistake: Ambivalent means mixed feelings, not no feelings. If you don't care, you're 'indifferent'.
origin: Latin 'ambi-', both, and 'valere', to be strong: two feelings pulling with equal strength.

upgrade.plain: I have mixed feelings about moving to the new office.
upgrade.model: I'm ambivalent about moving to the new office.

definition: Not certain or fixed; done hesitantly or provisionally.

examples.text: We've pencilled in a tentative date for the presentation, pending the tutor's approval.
That's a tentative answer; can you tell me why you think it's right?
Our tentative plan is to migrate in March, but it depends on the vendor.
We've made tentative plans for a weekend in Bath.

synonyms.note: Arranged for now and likely to change; more formal.
About a person's manner rather than a plan.

origin: Latin 'tentare', to try or test: the same root as 'attempt'.

upgrade.plain: We've agreed on a date, but it might change.
upgrade.model: We've agreed on a tentative date.

definition: Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible.

examples.text: The library's silent floor is far more conducive to revision than my flat.
Rearranging the desks into groups was more conducive to discussion.
Back-to-back meetings aren't conducive to deep work.
A noisy house isn't conducive to a good night's sleep.

synonyms.note: Broader; good for something in general.

commonMistake: It's always 'conducive to', never 'conducive for'.
origin: Latin 'conducere', to lead together: things that lead towards a result.

upgrade.plain: This noisy office doesn't help people concentrate.
upgrade.model: This noisy office isn't conducive to concentration.

definition: Showing good judgement, especially about quality.

examples.text: A discerning reader will notice that the author never defines 'success'.
Year 11 are becoming more discerning about which sources they trust online.
Our users are discerning; they'll notice if the app feels sluggish.
My dad is a discerning tea drinker; supermarket teabags won't do.

synonyms.note: Quick to notice and understand; not necessarily about quality.
Choosy; can imply simply being fussy.

origin: Latin 'discernere', to separate or distinguish.

upgrade.plain: Our customers have good taste and notice quality.
upgrade.model: Our customers are discerning.

definition: Without intending to; by accident.

examples.text: I inadvertently submitted the draft instead of the final version.
By giving the answer away, I inadvertently made the task too easy.
The migration inadvertently deleted test accounts in staging.
I inadvertently sent the photo to the whole family group chat.

synonyms.note: Stresses not knowing at the time.

origin: Latin 'in-', not, and 'advertere', to turn towards: not turning your attention to something.

upgrade.plain: I accidentally sent the email to the whole team.
upgrade.model: I inadvertently sent the email to the whole team.

definition: To estimate or judge something, such as a feeling, a situation or an amount.

examples.text: We ran a short survey to gauge interest before booking the venue.
I use exit tickets to gauge how well the class has understood.
Let's release to 5% of users first to gauge the impact on performance.
It's hard to gauge how long the queue will take.

synonyms.note: More general; can imply forming a firm opinion.

commonMistake: Spelt 'gauge' (a before u), not 'guage'. Pronounced like 'gage'.
origin: Old French 'gauger', to measure the contents of a barrel.

upgrade.plain: It's hard to tell how people feel about the change.
upgrade.model: It's hard to gauge how people feel about the change.

definition: To make something bad less severe or serious.

examples.text: The university extended the deadline to mitigate the impact of the strike.
Seating plans can mitigate a lot of low-level disruption.
We've added rate limiting to mitigate the risk of abuse.
We left early to mitigate the risk of traffic on the M25.

synonyms.note: Usually about suffering or a problem people feel.

commonMistake: Don't say 'mitigate against': you 'mitigate a risk' but 'militate against' an outcome.
origin: Latin 'mitis', soft or gentle: to soften something.

upgrade.plain: We added backups to make the risk smaller.
upgrade.model: We added backups to mitigate the risk.

definition: To make a problem, bad situation or feeling worse.

examples.text: Cutting the reading list would only exacerbate the gap between groups.
Raising my voice tends to exacerbate the situation rather than calm it.
Retrying immediately exacerbates the load on a server that's already struggling.
Scratching will only exacerbate the rash.

synonyms.note: Similar, but in everyday speech also means 'annoy'.
To add to an existing problem, making it bigger.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'exasperate', which means to annoy someone intensely.
origin: Latin 'acerbus', harsh or bitter: to make something more bitter.

upgrade.plain: Adding more people late will make the delay worse.
upgrade.model: Adding more people late will only exacerbate the delay.

definition: To make suffering, a problem or a difficulty less severe.

examples.text: A clear rubric would alleviate a lot of anxiety about the assessment.
A worked example on the board can alleviate the panic when pupils first see the question.
Caching the results should alleviate the pressure on the database.
A hot-water bottle helps alleviate the back pain.

synonyms.note: Very close; often about pain or worry.
More about reducing risk or damage.

origin: Latin 'levis', light: to make something lighter to carry.

upgrade.plain: Extra staff would ease the pressure on the team.
upgrade.model: Extra staff would alleviate the pressure on the team.

definition: Seeming reasonable or probable.

examples.text: It's a plausible interpretation, but you need evidence from the text to support it.
Before calculating, decide what a plausible answer would look like.
A race condition is the most plausible explanation for the intermittent failures.
'The dog ate it' isn't a plausible excuse for forgetting a birthday.

synonyms.note: Believable, often about a person or source.
Possible to do, rather than believable.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of a person: seemingly honest and convincing, but perhaps not to be trusted.
otherMeanings.example: He was a plausible rogue who talked his way into the job.
otherMeanings.cue: About a person, 'plausible' can carry a hint of suspicion.

origin: Latin 'plaudere', to applaud: originally 'deserving applause'.

upgrade.plain: That sounds like a believable reason.
upgrade.model: That's a perfectly plausible explanation.

definition: Clear and definite enough to be seen or measured; real.

examples.text: The placement gave me tangible experience to talk about in interviews.
Using blocks makes fractions tangible for younger pupils.
We need tangible results by the end of the sprint, not just research notes.
Walking to work has made a tangible difference to my energy.

synonyms.note: Specific and definite; very close in meaning.
So strong it can almost be felt, e.g. palpable tension.

origin: Latin 'tangere', to touch: something you could touch.

upgrade.plain: The new process has made a real, visible difference.
upgrade.model: The new process has made a tangible difference.

definition: Cautious because of possible dangers or problems.

examples.text: I'm wary of citing that blog; it isn't peer-reviewed.
Pupils are often wary of negative numbers until they see them on a number line.
I'm wary of adding another dependency just for one helper function.
I'm wary of texts asking for my bank details.

synonyms.note: Stronger; believing something may be wrong or dishonest.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'weary' (tired). 'Wary' rhymes with 'hairy'; 'weary' rhymes with 'theory'.
origin: From Old English 'wær', aware or careful: the same root as 'beware'.

upgrade.plain: I'm a bit careful about promising a date.
upgrade.model: I'm wary of committing to a date.

definition: To admit, often reluctantly, that something is true or that you have lost an argument.

examples.text: I'll concede that the counter-argument is strong, but it ignores the long-term costs.
She conceded that her method was longer, but it was just as valid.
I concede the point: the old API is simpler for this use case.
I'll concede that your shortcut was quicker.

synonyms.note: Plainer; not necessarily in an argument.
'I grant you that…': conversational and slightly old-fashioned.

otherMeanings.meaning: In sport, to let the other side score.
otherMeanings.example: England conceded a goal in the final minute.
otherMeanings.cue: Very common in football and cricket commentary.

origin: Latin 'concedere', to give way or yield.

upgrade.plain: OK, you're right about that bit.
upgrade.model: I'll concede that point.

definition: To try hard to do or achieve something (also a noun: a serious attempt).

examples.text: I will endeavour to submit the revised chapter by Friday.
We endeavour to reply to all parent emails within two working days.
We'll endeavour to resolve critical incidents within four hours.
I'll endeavour to arrive on time for once.

synonyms.note: Similar, with more sense of struggle.
Focuses on the goal rather than the effort.

commonMistake: British spelling is 'endeavour'; 'endeavor' is American.
origin: Middle English 'put oneself in devoir', to do one's duty, from French 'devoir'.

upgrade.plain: We'll try to get back to you by Monday.
upgrade.model: We'll endeavour to get back to you by Monday.

definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulties or withstand pressure.

examples.text: After failing the first module, she proved remarkably resilient and passed with a merit.
We want pupils to be resilient learners who see mistakes as part of the process.
The service needs to be resilient to a single region going down.
Kids are remarkably resilient after a house move.

synonyms.note: Strong and hard to break; often for systems.
Informal; can mean hard rather than adaptable.
Able to change to fit new conditions.

origin: Latin 'resilire', to leap back, like a spring.

upgrade.plain: The team bounced back quickly after the setback.
upgrade.model: The team proved resilient after the setback.

definition: To encourage the development of something, such as an idea, feeling or skill.

examples.text: The society aims to foster debate between students from different courses.
Open-ended problems foster curiosity far better than worksheets do.
Pairing sessions help foster a culture of knowledge sharing.
The community garden fosters a real sense of belonging on our street.

synonyms.note: Warmer; suggests care over a long period.
More active and public; to support or advertise.

otherMeanings.meaning: To look after a child who isn't legally yours, usually for a time.
otherMeanings.example: They've fostered over twenty children in the last ten years.
otherMeanings.cue: With a child or a pet as the object, it means caring for them, not encouraging them.

origin: Old English 'fostrian', to feed or nourish.

upgrade.plain: We want to encourage people to work together more.
upgrade.model: We want to foster collaboration across the team.

definition: To make it difficult for someone to do something or for something to happen.

examples.text: Poor Wi-Fi in halls really hindered my revision.
Too much text on a slide can hinder understanding rather than help it.
Flaky tests are hindering our ability to release quickly.
The snow hindered our journey home.

synonyms.note: Very close; often about movement or progress.

commonMistake: Pronounced with a short 'i', as in 'tinder', not like 'hind'.
origin: Old English 'hindrian', to hold back: related to 'behind'.

upgrade.plain: The constant interruptions slowed down our progress.
upgrade.model: The constant interruptions hindered our progress.

definition: Acting with care and thought for the future; sensible.

examples.text: It would be prudent to back up your dissertation somewhere other than your laptop.
It's prudent to check the equipment works before the observation lesson.
Given the risk, it seems prudent to take a database snapshot before the migration.
It would be prudent to book the restaurant in advance.

synonyms.note: Broader; suggests experience and good judgement.

origin: Latin 'providens', foreseeing: the same root as 'provide'.

upgrade.plain: It would be sensible to check with legal first.
upgrade.model: It would be prudent to check with legal first.

definition: Extremely complex and difficult to follow.

examples.text: The argument is so convoluted that I lost track of the main point.
That explanation was a bit convoluted; let me try it with a diagram.
The checkout logic has become convoluted after years of quick fixes.
The instructions for the flat-pack wardrobe were incredibly convoluted.

synonyms.note: Full of twists; often used about long processes.
Excessively complicated, especially rules or bureaucracy.

origin: Latin 'convolvere', to roll together: coiled like a snail shell.

upgrade.plain: The instructions are really complicated and hard to follow.
upgrade.model: The instructions are needlessly convoluted.

definition: Very convincing or interesting, demanding attention.

examples.text: You make a compelling case, but the data only covers one year.
A compelling hook at the start of the lesson can buy you twenty minutes of focus.
The performance numbers are a compelling argument for switching frameworks.
The estate agent made a compelling case for the bigger house.

synonyms.note: Convincing; focuses on changing someone's mind.
Exciting to watch or read; not about argument.

origin: Latin 'compellere', to drive together: an argument that drives you towards a conclusion.

upgrade.plain: She gave a very convincing reason to change the plan.
upgrade.model: She made a compelling case for changing the plan.

definition: Anxious or worried that something bad might happen.

examples.text: I'm a bit apprehensive about presenting to the whole department.
Some parents are apprehensive about the move to secondary school.
The team is apprehensive about the Friday release, given last month's outage.
I'm a bit apprehensive about meeting his parents.

synonyms.note: Everyday; can be about excitement too.
A vague sense that something is wrong.
Feeling a task is too big; less about danger.

origin: Latin 'apprehendere', to seize or grasp: the mind grasping at what might happen.

upgrade.plain: I'm a little worried about the interview.
upgrade.model: I'm slightly apprehensive about the interview.

definition: Showing care and steady effort in your work or duties.

examples.text: She's been diligent about revising a little every day since October.
He's a diligent pupil who always completes his homework, but he needs more stretch.
Thanks for being so diligent with the documentation; it saved the new starter days.
Our neighbour is diligent about sorting the recycling.

synonyms.note: Stresses wanting to do a job properly and honestly.

origin: Latin 'diligere', to value or love: you take care over what you value.

upgrade.plain: He's been very hard-working and careful this term.
upgrade.model: He's been exceptionally diligent this term.

definition: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively (as a verb, /ɑːˈtɪkjuleɪt/: to express clearly).

examples.text: He's very articulate in seminars, but his essays don't yet reflect it.
I want you to articulate your reasoning, not just give the answer.
She's brilliant at articulating technical trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders.
My niece is very articulate for a six-year-old.

synonyms.note: Very clear and easy to understand; used about explanations.
Speaks clearly and politely; about manner more than ideas.

commonMistake: The adjective ends '-ulət'; the verb ends '-ulate' like 'late'.
origin: Latin 'articulus', small joint: speech divided into clear, jointed parts.

upgrade.plain: Can you explain clearly why you chose this design?
upgrade.model: Can you articulate why you chose this design?

definition: To confirm or support a statement, theory or finding with further evidence.

examples.text: Two later studies corroborate her findings, which strengthens your argument.
Can we corroborate our prediction by repeating the experiment with a different mass?
The server logs corroborate the user's report: the request timed out at 14:02.
My neighbour corroborated my story about the broken fence.

synonyms.note: To provide evidence for a claim that had none.

origin: Latin 'corroborare', to strengthen, from 'robur', oak (the root of 'robust').

upgrade.plain: Other research backs up what she found.
upgrade.model: Other research corroborates her findings.

definition: To provide evidence to show that something is true.

examples.text: That's a bold claim; you'll need to substantiate it with primary sources.
Good answer. Can you substantiate it with a number from the graph?
Can we substantiate the claim that users want dark mode, or is it a hunch?
The insurer asked me to substantiate my claim with receipts.

synonyms.note: Confirms something that already has some evidence.

origin: Latin 'substantia', substance: giving a claim real substance.

upgrade.plain: You need to show evidence for what you're saying.
upgrade.model: You need to substantiate your claim.

definition: To combine ideas or information from different sources into a coherent whole.

examples.text: A good literature review synthesises the research rather than summarising each paper in turn.
In the final task, pupils synthesise what they've learnt about forces and energy.
I've synthesised the feedback from all five user interviews into three themes.
I synthesised everyone's holiday wishes into one plan.

synonyms.note: Plainer; doesn't imply creating something new.
To bring parts into a working whole.
Not the same: summarising shortens, synthesising connects.

otherMeanings.meaning: In chemistry, to make a compound from simpler substances.
otherMeanings.example: Aspirin was first synthesised in 1897.

commonMistake: British spelling is usually 'synthesise'; 'synthesize' is American (and Oxford) style.
origin: Greek 'synthesis', putting together.

upgrade.plain: I put together the ideas from the three articles.
upgrade.model: I synthesised the ideas from the three articles.

definition: Clear, logical and convincing.

examples.text: Your examiner wants a cogent argument, not a list of everything you know.
That was a cogent explanation of why the reaction speeds up.
She made a cogent case for splitting the monolith into two services.
My teenager made a surprisingly cogent case for a later bedtime.

synonyms.note: Plainer; about the effect on the listener.
Logically connected, but not necessarily persuasive.

origin: Latin 'cogere', to drive together or compel.

upgrade.plain: He gave a clear and convincing argument.
upgrade.model: He gave a cogent argument.

definition: To put forward an idea or assumption as a basis for argument.

examples.text: Freud posits that dreams reveal unconscious desires.
Darwin posited that species change over time through natural selection.
The design doc posits that most reads will hit the cache.
My brother posits that cereal is technically a soup.

synonyms.note: More general; also used for plans.

origin: Latin 'ponere', to place: to place an idea on the table.

upgrade.plain: The author suggests that money doesn't make people happier.
upgrade.model: The author posits that money doesn't make people happier.

definition: To place two things side by side, especially to highlight a contrast.

examples.text: The poet juxtaposes images of war with scenes from childhood.
Juxtapose the two graphs: what do you notice about the gradients?
The dashboard juxtaposes last week's error rate with this week's.
The restaurant juxtaposes old oak beams with very modern lighting.

synonyms.note: Focuses on differences, without the physical side-by-side sense.

origin: French 'juxtaposer', from Latin 'juxta', next to.

upgrade.plain: The film puts rich and poor families next to each other.
upgrade.model: The film juxtaposes rich and poor families.

definition: To evaluate something in a detailed, analytical way (also a noun: such an evaluation).

examples.text: In part two, critique the methodology: what are its limitations?
Pupils critique each other's graphs using the success criteria.
Could you critique my architecture proposal before I share it wider?
My sister critiqued my wedding speech line by line.

synonyms.note: Usually means finding fault; 'critique' weighs strengths and weaknesses.
Neutral judgement of value or quality.

commonMistake: 'Critique' is a balanced evaluation; 'criticise' suggests negativity. Don't write 'critic' for the verb.
origin: French, from Greek 'kritikē tekhnē', the art of judgement.

upgrade.plain: Look at the strengths and weaknesses of this study.
upgrade.model: Critique this study.

definition: To describe or mark out something precisely.

examples.text: The introduction should delineate the scope of your study.
The marking scheme clearly delineates what earns each mark.
The RFC delineates which team owns each part of the pipeline.
The tenancy agreement clearly delineates who pays for repairs.

synonyms.note: To state the exact meaning or limits.
Neutral, British; to present in an organised way.

origin: Latin 'delineare', to sketch out, from 'linea', line.

upgrade.plain: The contract clearly shows who is responsible for what.
upgrade.model: The contract clearly delineates responsibilities.

definition: Logical and consistent, so the parts fit together clearly.

examples.text: Each paragraph is good on its own, but the essay doesn't yet feel coherent.
We want a coherent curriculum where Year 8 builds on Year 7.
The API needs a coherent naming scheme; right now every endpoint is different.
After the night feed, I wasn't very coherent.

synonyms.note: Focuses on reasoning rather than overall shape.
Parts stick together; often used about teams or texts.

origin: Latin 'cohaerere', to stick together.

upgrade.plain: Your plan needs to make sense as a whole.
upgrade.model: Your plan needs to be coherent.

definition: Most noticeable or important.

examples.text: Summarise the salient points of the case in under 200 words.
Highlight the salient information in the question before you start.
Here are the salient details from the incident report.
Just give me the salient points of the plot; I've missed three episodes.

synonyms.note: Relevant to the matter at hand.

origin: Latin 'salire', to leap: points that jump out at you.

upgrade.plain: Just tell me the main points.
upgrade.model: Just give me the salient points.

definition: A typical model or pattern of thinking, especially one accepted in a field.

examples.text: Kuhn argued that science advances through paradigm shifts.
The move from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model was a paradigm shift.
React introduced a declarative paradigm for building interfaces.
Online food shopping was a paradigm shift for my parents.

synonyms.note: A structure of ideas or rules.

commonMistake: The 'g' is silent: 'PA-ra-dime'. 'Paradigm shift' is overused in business; save it for genuinely fundamental changes.
origin: Greek 'paradeigma', pattern or example.

upgrade.plain: Remote work has completely changed how we think about offices.
upgrade.model: Remote work has caused a paradigm shift in how we think about offices.

definition: Based on observation or experiment rather than theory alone.

examples.text: There's little empirical evidence that learning styles exist.
Science is empirical: we test ideas against what we actually observe.
Let's get empirical data from a load test before we argue about the bottleneck.
My empirical research shows the 8.15 train is always late.

origin: Greek 'empeiria', experience.

upgrade.plain: We need real data from tests, not guesses.
upgrade.model: We need empirical data, not guesses.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not clear.

examples.text: The essay question is ambiguous; I'll email the tutor to check.
'Find the difference' is ambiguous to some pupils; we mean subtract.
The requirement is ambiguous: does 'recent' mean the last day or the last week?
The sign was ambiguous: did 'no parking' include Sundays?

synonyms.note: Plainer; may be confusing rather than double-meaning.
Lacking detail, rather than having two meanings.
Formal; deliberately unclear to avoid commitment.

origin: Latin 'ambigere', to waver or go around.

upgrade.plain: The instructions could mean two different things.
upgrade.model: The instructions are ambiguous.

definition: Suggested or understood without being stated directly.

examples.text: There's an implicit criticism of the government in the final chapter.
The question has an implicit step: you need to find the area first.
The function has an implicit dependency on the system time zone.
There was an implicit invitation to stay for dinner.

synonyms.note: Very close; 'implicit' can also mean complete, as in implicit trust.
Understood without words, e.g. tacit agreement.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of trust or faith: complete and unquestioning.
otherMeanings.example: I have implicit trust in her judgement.
otherMeanings.cue: 'Implicit trust', 'implicit faith' and 'implicit confidence' mean total, not hinted at.

origin: Latin 'implicare', to fold in: meaning folded inside the words.

upgrade.plain: There's a hidden assumption in your plan.
upgrade.model: There's an implicit assumption in your plan.

definition: Existing as a natural, permanent part of something.

examples.text: Self-reported surveys have inherent limitations.
Every measurement has some inherent uncertainty.
Distributed systems have inherent trade-offs between consistency and availability.
There's an inherent risk in buying a second-hand car.

synonyms.note: Belonging to the essential nature; very close.
Present from birth; used for people and abilities.

origin: Latin 'inhaerere', to stick in.

upgrade.plain: There's always some risk in starting a business.
upgrade.model: Starting a business carries inherent risk.

definition: To weaken something gradually or secretly.

examples.text: One weak source can undermine an otherwise strong essay.
Inconsistent rules undermine pupils' trust in the behaviour policy.
Skipping code review undermines everything we've built around quality.
Constant teasing can undermine a child's confidence.

origin: Literally to dig a mine under a castle wall, making it collapse.

upgrade.plain: Changing the deadline again makes people trust us less.
upgrade.model: Changing the deadline again undermines trust.

definition: To claim or argue that something is true; also, to deal with a difficulty ('contend with').

examples.text: I contend that the policy failed because of poor funding, not poor design.
New teachers have a lot to contend with in their first term.
We also have to contend with a legacy database nobody fully understands.
With three kids and a dog, we have a lot to contend with in the mornings.

collocations: have a lot to contend with

synonyms.note: For the 'deal with' sense; stresses struggle.

origin: Latin 'contendere', to strive or stretch.

upgrade.plain: Some people say that homework doesn't help.
upgrade.model: Some researchers contend that homework doesn't help.

definition: To agree with someone or have the same opinion.

examples.text: Most critics concur that it's her finest novel.
I concur with the head of department; the results speak for themselves.
I concur. Let's go with option B and revisit after the beta.
My GP concurred that rest was the best treatment.

commonMistake: Can sound stiff in casual speech. Use it in writing or formal meetings, and 'agree' with friends.
origin: Latin 'concurrere', to run together.

upgrade.plain: I agree with Sam's suggestion.
upgrade.model: I concur with Sam's suggestion.

definition: To make something clear by explaining it.

examples.text: Could you elucidate what you mean by 'cultural capital'?
This diagram should elucidate how the heart pumps blood.
The README elucidates the deploy process far better than the old wiki did.
The pharmacist elucidated the difference between the two medicines.

origin: Latin 'lucidus', bright: to bring into the light.

upgrade.plain: Can you explain that point more clearly?
upgrade.model: Could you elucidate that point?

definition: To prove that a statement or theory is wrong.

examples.text: The new data refutes the idea that the decline began in 2010.
Galileo's experiments refuted the belief that heavier objects fall faster.
The benchmark refutes the claim that the ORM is the bottleneck.
The photos refute his claim that he'd tidied his room.

synonyms.note: To argue against, without necessarily proving.
To say something isn't true, without proof.

commonMistake: 'Refute' means prove wrong, not just deny. If you only disagree, use 'reject', 'deny' or 'dispute'.
origin: Latin 'refutare', to drive back.

upgrade.plain: The test results prove that theory wrong.
upgrade.model: The test results refute that theory.

definition: A difference between things that should match.

examples.text: There's a discrepancy between the figures in your table and in your text.
Can anyone explain the discrepancy between our result and the textbook value?
We found a discrepancy between the invoice totals and the payments table.
There's a discrepancy between the menu price and the bill.

synonyms.note: Broader; things that contradict each other.
A large, often unfair, difference, e.g. a pay disparity.

origin: Latin 'discrepare', to sound differently or be out of tune.

upgrade.plain: The two reports don't match.
upgrade.model: There's a discrepancy between the two reports.

definition: Coming before the main part of something; initial.

examples.text: My preliminary findings suggest the effect is stronger in older groups.
Before the full investigation, run a preliminary test to check your timings.
Preliminary results from the A/B test look promising.
The preliminary quote for the new boiler was higher than we'd hoped.

origin: Latin 'prae', before, and 'limen', threshold: before you step over the doorstep.

upgrade.plain: These are early results, so they might change.
upgrade.model: These are preliminary results.

definition: Including all or nearly all aspects of something.

examples.text: The review gives a comprehensive overview of the last decade of research.
The revision guide is comprehensive, but pupils find it overwhelming.
We need comprehensive test coverage on the payments module.
The guidebook has a comprehensive list of coastal walks.

synonyms.note: Focuses on care rather than range.
Covers absolutely everything; can sound tiring.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) In the UK, a state secondary school that doesn't select pupils by ability.
otherMeanings.example: I went to the local comprehensive, then to sixth-form college.
otherMeanings.cue: As a noun, 'a comprehensive' (or 'a comp') is the school.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'comprehensible' (understandable).
origin: Latin 'comprehendere', to grasp completely.

upgrade.plain: The guide covers everything you need.
upgrade.model: The guide is comprehensive.

definition: Although; used to add a limiting fact (a conjunction).

examples.text: The study was successful, albeit on a small scale.
She got the right answer, albeit by a rather roundabout method.
The fix works, albeit with a slight performance cost.
We had a lovely holiday, albeit a rainy one.

synonyms.note: More flexible; can introduce a full clause.
As in 'a useful, if limited, tool'.

commonMistake: 'Albeit' is followed by an adjective, adverb or phrase, not a full clause: 'albeit slowly', not 'albeit it was slow'.
origin: Middle English 'al be it', although it be.

upgrade.plain: It was a good result, but only a small one.
upgrade.model: It was a good result, albeit a modest one.

definition: By which; used to introduce a method or arrangement (a relative adverb).

examples.text: We introduced a system whereby each member reviews another's section.
Osmosis is the process whereby water moves across a partially permeable membrane.
We use a scheme whereby each service owns its own database.
We have an arrangement whereby I cook and he washes up.

origin: Middle English 'where' plus 'by': by what or by which.

upgrade.plain: We set up a system where everyone takes turns to lead.
upgrade.model: We set up a system whereby everyone takes turns to lead.

definition: To justify or make something necessary.

examples.text: The topic is broad enough to warrant a whole chapter.
One late homework doesn't warrant a detention.
A bug this minor doesn't warrant a hotfix; it can go in the next release.
A small scratch doesn't warrant a new phone.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) A legal document allowing the police to search, or to arrest someone.
otherMeanings.example: The police had a warrant to search the flat.

origin: Old French 'warantir', to guarantee: the same root as 'guarantee'.

upgrade.plain: These results are worth looking into more.
upgrade.model: These results warrant further investigation.

definition: To examine something very carefully and critically.

examples.text: Scrutinise your sources: who funded the study?
Ofsted will scrutinise pupils' books to see progress over time.
Security will scrutinise any change to the authentication code.
Always scrutinise the small print before signing a phone contract.

synonyms.note: Often official, e.g. a school inspection.
To read with great attention, often for a long time.

commonMistake: British spelling is 'scrutinise'; 'scrutinize' is American.
origin: Latin 'scrutari', to search through rubbish or rags.

upgrade.plain: The board will look very closely at the budget.
upgrade.model: The board will scrutinise the budget.

definition: To support or form the basis of an idea, argument or system.

examples.text: Two key assumptions underpin the author's model.
Times tables underpin almost everything they'll do in Year 7 maths.
This message queue underpins every service in the platform.
Trust underpins any good friendship.

origin: A building term: to support a wall from below.

upgrade.plain: Good data is the basis of every decision we make.
upgrade.model: Good data underpins every decision we make.

definition: The most important or difficult point of an issue.

examples.text: The crux of the debate is whether the benefits outweigh the costs.
This is the crux of the topic; if you get this, the rest follows.
The crux of the problem is that two services write to the same table.
The crux of the problem is that nobody wants to drive.

origin: Latin for 'cross': a puzzle at the crossing point.

upgrade.plain: The main issue is that we don't have enough time.
upgrade.model: The crux of the matter is that we don't have enough time.

definition: Very weak or slight; not convincing.

examples.text: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
That's a tenuous connection; can you find stronger evidence in the data?
The correlation between the deploy and the outage is tenuous; let's check the logs.
His excuse for missing the party was tenuous at best.

origin: Latin 'tenuis', thin.

upgrade.plain: The connection between these ideas is pretty weak.
upgrade.model: The connection between these ideas is tenuous.

definition: To support a learner with temporary structure or help, then gradually remove it as they become independent.

examples.text: The first assignment is heavily scaffolded, with a template for each section.
I'll scaffold the first two questions with sentence starters, then let them work independently.
We scaffolded the new starters' first week with small, well-defined tickets.
When teaching Gran to video-call, I scaffolded it: answering first, then calling.

synonyms.note: General; doesn't imply the help is temporary.
Focuses on the framework rather than the fading help.

commonMistake: In software, 'scaffold' also means to generate starter code (e.g. 'scaffold a project'); context makes the meaning clear.
origin: Old French 'escadafaut', a raised platform: support around a building until it can stand alone.

upgrade.plain: I'll give them some help at first, then less as they get better.
upgrade.model: I'll scaffold the task and gradually remove the support.

definition: To suggest an explanation that can then be tested.

examples.text: We hypothesise that sleep quality affects exam performance.
Before we heat the water, hypothesise what will happen to the dissolving time.
We hypothesise that the shorter sign-up form will increase conversions by 5%.
I hypothesise that the cat is being fed next door too.

synonyms.note: States an outcome; doesn't need an explanation.
Guess, without the intention to test.
Put forward as a basis for argument.

commonMistake: Plural of 'hypothesis' is 'hypotheses' (hy-POTH-uh-seez). British spelling: 'hypothesise'.
origin: Greek 'hypothesis', a foundation or supposition: literally 'placing under'.

upgrade.plain: We think that more light will make the plant grow faster.
upgrade.model: We hypothesise that more light will make the plant grow faster.

definition: A belief that is wrong because it is based on faulty thinking or understanding.

examples.text: A common misconception is that Victorians thought the world was flat.
A classic misconception is that multiplying always makes a number bigger.
There's a misconception that adding more servers always makes things faster.
It's a common misconception that bulls hate the colour red.

synonyms.note: A mistaken belief based on unsound argument.
A widely held but false belief.

origin: Mis- (wrongly) plus 'conception', from Latin 'concipere', to take in.

upgrade.plain: Lots of pupils wrongly think heavier things fall faster.
upgrade.model: A common misconception is that heavier things fall faster.

definition: To estimate something beyond the known data by assuming the trend continues.

examples.text: You can't extrapolate from one interview to the whole population.
Extend the line of best fit to extrapolate the temperature at ten minutes.
If we extrapolate current growth, we'll run out of disk space by June.
Don't extrapolate from one rainy day; the holiday might still be lovely.

synonyms.note: Estimate within the range of known data; the opposite direction.
Forecast future figures; common in business.

commonMistake: Extrapolate means beyond the data; estimating between known points is 'interpolate'.
origin: Extra- (outside) plus 'interpolate': estimating outside the known points.

upgrade.plain: If we continue the trend, we'll hit 1,000 users next month.
upgrade.model: If we extrapolate the trend, we'll hit 1,000 users next month.

definition: To make knowledge, a position or a system stronger and more secure, often by combining parts.

examples.text: I use flashcards to consolidate what I've covered in lectures.
Today is a consolidation lesson: no new content, just practice.
Let's consolidate the three config files into one.
I consolidated my three old pensions into one.

synonyms.note: Combine into one; no sense of strengthening.

origin: Latin 'consolidare', to make solid.

upgrade.plain: This homework will help them remember what we did today.
upgrade.model: This homework will consolidate today's learning.

definition: To tell things apart; in teaching, to adapt a task so learners with different needs can all access it.

examples.text: Can you differentiate between correlation and causation in your answer?
I differentiate the worksheet three ways: support, core and challenge.
What really differentiates our product is the offline mode.
Can you differentiate between a crow and a rook?

synonyms.note: For the teaching sense; more general.
Adjust to suit a particular person.

otherMeanings.meaning: In maths, to find the derivative of a function.
otherMeanings.example: Differentiate y = x² to find the gradient at any point.
otherMeanings.cue: In a maths department, say 'adapt the task' for the teaching sense, to avoid confusion.

origin: Latin 'differentia', difference.

upgrade.plain: I made easier and harder versions of the task.
upgrade.model: I differentiated the task for different ability levels.

definition: To draw out a response, answer or reaction from someone.

examples.text: The interview questions were designed to elicit honest answers.
Rather than telling them the rule, try to elicit it from the examples.
Good discovery sessions elicit requirements users didn't know they had.
My joke finally elicited a smile from the grumpy bus driver.

synonyms.note: Bring a feeling or memory to mind.
Get something out, often with effort or reluctance.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'illicit' (illegal). They sound almost the same.
origin: Latin 'elicere', to draw out or entice.

upgrade.plain: Ask questions to get the answer out of them rather than telling them.
upgrade.model: Ask questions to elicit the answer rather than telling them.

definition: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from known facts.

examples.text: From the diary entries, we can deduce that she left London in 1851.
Using the angles you know, deduce the missing angle and explain each step.
From the stack trace, I deduced the bug was in the date parser.
From the muddy paw prints, I deduced the dog had been on the sofa.

synonyms.note: Reach a conclusion from evidence, often less strictly logical.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'deduct' (to subtract money or points).
origin: Latin 'deducere', to lead down: leading down from facts to a conclusion.

upgrade.plain: From the clues, we can work out who did it.
upgrade.model: From the clues, we can deduce who did it.

definition: Different from what is normal or expected.

examples.text: One anomalous result skewed the average, so we excluded it with justification.
Circle any anomalous results on your graph and suggest a reason for them.
The monitoring flagged anomalous traffic from a single IP address.
The anomalous payment on my bank statement turned out to be fraud.

synonyms.note: Not typical; often used in medicine and research.
Noun: a data point far from the others.

origin: Greek 'anomalos', uneven.

upgrade.plain: This result is really different from the others.
upgrade.model: This result is anomalous.

definition: A connection between two things, where one tends to change as the other does.

examples.text: There's a strong correlation between attendance and final grade.
Correlation doesn't prove causation: ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer.
We see a correlation between page load time and drop-off rate.
There's a clear correlation between my mood and how much sleep I get.

synonyms.note: Common in research; a looser connection.
Not a synonym: one thing causing another.

origin: Latin 'cor-', together, plus 'relatio', a bringing back.

upgrade.plain: People who sleep more tend to get better marks.
upgrade.model: There's a correlation between sleep and marks.

definition: To express or measure the amount of something.

examples.text: It's hard to quantify the impact of social media on wellbeing.
Don't just say it got faster; quantify it: by how many seconds?
Can we quantify the cost of the outage in lost orders?
It's hard to quantify how much our neighbour helps us.

origin: Latin 'quantus', how much.

upgrade.plain: Can you put a number on how much time this saves?
upgrade.model: Can you quantify how much time this saves?

definition: Extremely thorough, careful and accurate.

examples.text: The methodology needs to be more rigorous for a journal submission.
A rigorous proof covers every case, not just the examples you tried.
We put every release through rigorous automated testing.
My mum is rigorous about checking use-by dates.

synonyms.note: Plainer; complete but not necessarily strict.
Strict, usually about rules or standards.

commonMistake: British spelling: 'rigour' (noun) but 'rigorous' (adjective), with no 'u' in the adjective.
origin: Latin 'rigor', stiffness: unbending standards.

upgrade.plain: We need to test this really carefully and properly.
upgrade.model: We need to test this rigorously.

definition: Different from what common sense would lead you to expect.

examples.text: It seems counter-intuitive, but taking breaks improves revision.
It's counter-intuitive, but a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate in a vacuum.
It's counter-intuitive, but adding an index slowed this particular query down.
It's counter-intuitive, but a hot drink can help you cool down.

commonMistake: British style often hyphenates it ('counter-intuitive'); 'counterintuitive' is also accepted.
origin: Counter- (against) plus 'intuitive', from Latin 'intueri', to look at.

upgrade.plain: It's surprising, but slowing down can help you finish sooner.
upgrade.model: It's counter-intuitive, but slowing down can help you finish sooner.

definition: To come close to a value without being exact (adjective /əˈprɒksɪmət/: roughly correct).

examples.text: The approximate word count is 3,000, give or take ten per cent.
We can approximate pi as 3.14 for this question.
The model approximates user behaviour well enough for capacity planning.
The approximate journey time to Leeds is two hours.

synonyms.note: Maths: adjust to a simpler value.

commonMistake: Verb ends '-mate' (like 'late'); adjective ends '-mət'.
origin: Latin 'proximus', nearest.

upgrade.plain: The answer is roughly 40.
upgrade.model: The answer is approximately 40.

definition: Corresponding in size or amount to something else; in maths, increasing or decreasing at the same rate.

examples.text: The punishment should be proportional to the offence.
If y is directly proportional to x, doubling x doubles y.
Costs grow proportional to the number of active users.
The tip should be proportional to the bill.

origin: Latin 'pro portione', according to its share.

upgrade.plain: The force increases at the same rate as the stretch.
upgrade.model: The force is directly proportional to the extension.

definition: Ongoing checks on learning used to adjust teaching, rather than to give a final grade.

examples.text: The weekly quizzes are formative assessment; they don't count towards your grade.
Hinge questions are a quick form of formative assessment mid-lesson.
Code review works like formative assessment: feedback to improve, not to grade.
My son's school uses weekly quizzes as formative assessment, so they don't count towards his grades.

synonyms.note: The opposite: a final judgement, e.g. an exam.

origin: Latin 'formare', to shape: assessment that shapes the learning.

upgrade.plain: I use quick quizzes to see what they understand so I can change my teaching.
upgrade.model: I use quick quizzes as formative assessment.

definition: What a learner already knows before a new topic is taught.

examples.text: The module assumes prior knowledge of basic statistics.
Let's activate prior knowledge: what do you remember about atoms from Year 7?
The onboarding guide assumes no prior knowledge of Kubernetes.
The pub quiz assumed a lot of prior knowledge about 1980s pop.

origin: Latin 'prior', earlier.

upgrade.plain: No experience needed; we'll start from the basics.
upgrade.model: No prior knowledge is assumed.

definition: To be a typical example of something, or to illustrate it with examples.

examples.text: This speech exemplifies the rhetoric of the period.
Let me exemplify this with a worked example on the board.
This module exemplifies the coding standards we want everywhere.
Our street party exemplifies real community spirit.

synonyms.note: Represent a quality fully, usually a person.

origin: Latin 'exemplum', example.

upgrade.plain: Her work is a perfect example of what we're looking for.
upgrade.model: Her work exemplifies what we're looking for.

definition: To say something again, usually for emphasis or clarity.

examples.text: In your conclusion, don't just reiterate your introduction.
I'll reiterate the key point: always show your working.
Just to reiterate, the code freeze starts on Thursday at 5 p.m.
Just to reiterate: the taxi comes at six, not seven.

synonyms.note: Say again, often in different words.

commonMistake: 'Reiterate again' is redundant: 'reiterate' already means 'say again'.
origin: Latin 're-', again, and 'iterare', to repeat: repeat again.

upgrade.plain: I'll say it again because it's important.
upgrade.model: I'll reiterate this because it's important.

definition: To analyse something complicated by breaking it into parts and explaining each.

examples.text: Let's unpack the essay question before we start planning.
This is a tricky exam question, so let's unpack it line by line.
Can you unpack what 'scalable' means for this particular feature?
Let's unpack why the holiday plans fell through.

origin: A metaphor from opening a suitcase and taking things out one by one.

upgrade.plain: Can you explain that idea in more detail, step by step?
upgrade.model: Can you unpack that idea a bit?

definition: Helpful and intended to improve something, rather than just criticise it.

examples.text: My supervisor's comments were tough but constructive.
When you peer-mark, give one piece of praise and one constructive suggestion.
Keep review comments constructive: suggest a fix, not just a problem.
My friend gave me some constructive feedback on my wedding speech.

origin: Latin 'construere', to build: feedback that builds rather than destroys.

upgrade.plain: Thanks for your helpful comments on how to improve it.
upgrade.model: Thanks for your constructive feedback.

definition: To set something, such as a lesson or explanation, at a particular level of difficulty.

examples.text: The lecture was pitched at second-years, so I struggled to follow.
The lesson was pitched too high for a Year 8 set; I'll adjust it next time.
Pitch the demo at the business audience, not the engineers.
The cookery class was pitched at total beginners, which suited me.

collocations: pitch it at the right level

synonyms.note: Direct at a target audience; less about level of difficulty.
Common phrase for getting the level exactly right.
A different sense: a persuasive presentation, e.g. a sales pitch.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) A sports field.
otherMeanings.example: The match was called off because the pitch was waterlogged.
otherMeanings.cue: British English says 'football pitch' and 'cricket pitch', not 'field'.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) A persuasive presentation, for example to win business.
otherMeanings.example: We've got ten minutes to make our pitch to the investors.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) How high or low a sound is.
otherMeanings.example: Her voice rose in pitch when she got excited.

origin: From the sense of setting the musical pitch of a note: high or low.

upgrade.plain: The talk was too hard for the audience.
upgrade.model: The talk was pitched too high for the audience.

definition: To summarise the main points again (also a noun: a brief summary).

examples.text: Let's recap before we move on to the next chapter.
Quick recap: what are the three states of matter?
To recap: we're shipping on Tuesday and Sam owns the rollback plan.
Quick recap for anyone who missed last month's book club.

synonyms.note: Go over again, often in more detail.

origin: Short for 'recapitulate', from Latin 'capitulum', a chapter or heading.

upgrade.plain: So, to go over the main points again: we're on track.
upgrade.model: So, to recap: we're on track.

definition: To move towards the same point or come together; in maths, to approach a limit.

examples.text: Our views converged after a long discussion.
As n gets bigger, the sequence converges to 1.
The two teams' designs are starting to converge on one approach.
The whole family converges on Gran's house every Boxing Day.

origin: Latin 'con-', together, and 'vergere', to incline.

upgrade.plain: We're slowly agreeing on the same plan.
upgrade.model: We're slowly converging on the same plan.

definition: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.

examples.text: The difference between the two groups was negligible.
We can assume air resistance is negligible for this calculation.
The extra latency from logging is negligible.
The price difference between the two kettles is negligible.

synonyms.note: Of little importance; can sound dismissive.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'negligent' (careless in a way that causes harm).
origin: Latin 'neglegere', to disregard: small enough to ignore.

upgrade.plain: The cost of this change is so small it doesn't matter.
upgrade.model: The cost of this change is negligible.

definition: Opposite in position, direction or effect (also a noun: the opposite).

examples.text: There's an inverse relationship between price and demand.
Subtraction is the inverse of addition, so use it to check your answer.
The decode function is the inverse of encode; round-tripping should give the original.
There's an inverse relationship between my bank balance and the number of birthdays in June.

synonyms.note: Logic: swapping the parts of a statement.

origin: Latin 'inversus', turned upside down.

upgrade.plain: The more you practise, the fewer mistakes you make.
upgrade.model: There's an inverse relationship between practice and mistakes.

definition: To repeat or reproduce something exactly, such as an experiment or result.

examples.text: Other researchers have failed to replicate the original findings.
Write your method clearly enough that another group could replicate it.
I can't replicate the bug on my machine; can you share your browser version?
I've never managed to replicate my mum's roast potatoes.

synonyms.note: Very close; 'reproduce the bug' is common in software.
Make an exact copy; no sense of testing.

origin: Latin 'replicare', to fold back.

upgrade.plain: Can anyone else get the same result?
upgrade.model: Can anyone else replicate the result?

definition: Awareness and understanding of your own thinking and learning.

examples.text: Reflecting on why I got questions wrong has improved my metacognition.
Asking 'How did you check your answer?' builds metacognition.
Writing a post-mortem is an exercise in team metacognition: how did we think about the problem?
Noticing why I always forget people's names is a bit of metacognition.

synonyms.note: Managing your behaviour and learning, often paired with it.

origin: Greek 'meta', beyond, plus 'cognition': thinking about thinking.

upgrade.plain: I want pupils to think about how they learn best.
upgrade.model: I want to develop pupils' metacognition.

definition: UK teaching term for extending the most able learners beyond the core task.

examples.text: The extension reading list is there as stretch and challenge for anyone aiming for a first.
There's a stretch and challenge question at the bottom for anyone who finishes early.
We give interns a stretch and challenge task once they've completed the core onboarding.
My daughter's homework has a stretch and challenge question at the bottom.

origin: UK education jargon, popularised in Ofsted and school improvement literature.

upgrade.plain: I've added a harder question for pupils who finish quickly.
upgrade.model: I've added a stretch and challenge question for pupils who finish quickly.

definition: In UK teaching, the part at the end of a lesson that reviews what has been learnt.

examples.text: The conference ended with a plenary session for all delegates.
For the plenary, each group shares one thing they'd change about their method.
After the breakout sessions, we'll reconvene for a plenary to agree next steps.
The residents' meeting ended with a plenary where everyone voted on the new bins.

synonyms.note: Discussion after an event, often in work contexts.

otherMeanings.meaning: At a conference, a session attended by everyone, not just one group.
otherMeanings.example: The keynote talk is in the plenary session before lunch.
otherMeanings.cue: Outside schools it's conference-speak, not the end of a lesson.

origin: Latin 'plenus', full: a session where everyone is present.

upgrade.plain: At the end of the lesson, we'll go over what we learnt.
upgrade.model: In the plenary, we'll review what we've learnt.

definition: To improve something by repeating a cycle of making, testing and refining it.

examples.text: We iterated on the poster design three times after peer feedback.
I iterate on this lesson every year based on what pupils struggle with.
Let's ship a basic version and iterate based on user feedback.
I've iterated on my lasagne recipe for years.

synonyms.note: Improve in small ways; no sense of repeated cycles.
Change after reconsidering; common for documents.

origin: Latin 'iterum', again.

upgrade.plain: We'll keep improving it bit by bit after launch.
upgrade.model: We'll iterate on it after launch.

definition: In software, to mark a feature as outdated and due for removal; more generally, to express disapproval.

examples.text: The university deprecated the old portal, so submit through the new one.
That exam board specification has been deprecated; use the 2025 version.
We're deprecating v1 of the API and will remove it in six months.
My bank is deprecating its old app, so I need to download the new one.

synonyms.note: Business jargon for ending a product.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Self-deprecating': modestly making fun of yourself, a much-loved British trait.
otherMeanings.example: His self-deprecating humour put everyone at ease.

commonMistake: Don't confuse with 'depreciate' (to lose value over time).
origin: Latin 'deprecari', to pray against: to wish something away.

upgrade.plain: We're going to stop supporting the old version soon.
upgrade.model: We're deprecating the old version.

definition: A person or group with an interest in, or affected by, a project or decision.

examples.text: We interviewed every stakeholder, from students to catering staff.
Parents are key stakeholders in any change to the homework policy.
Let's get the key stakeholders together before we change the roadmap.
With three kids and two grandparents, every holiday has a lot of stakeholders.

synonyms.note: Only those with power to decide.

origin: Originally the person who held the money (the stakes) during a bet.

upgrade.plain: We need to talk to everyone affected by this change.
upgrade.model: We need to consult all the stakeholders.

definition: Informally at work, the time, energy or capacity to take on something.

examples.text: I don't have the bandwidth to join another society this term.
With reports due, I don't have the bandwidth for a new initiative this half-term.
Does anyone have the bandwidth to pick up this ticket this sprint?
I don't have the bandwidth for a dinner party this week.

otherMeanings.meaning: In computing, how much data a connection can carry.
otherMeanings.example: Streaming in 4K uses a lot of bandwidth.
otherMeanings.cue: About networks it's literal; about people it means time or capacity.

commonMistake: Fine in tech workplaces, but can sound like jargon elsewhere; with parents, say 'time' or 'capacity'.
origin: Originally the range of frequencies a signal can carry.

upgrade.plain: I don't have time to take this on right now.
upgrade.model: I don't have the bandwidth to take this on right now.

definition: A balance between two things you can't have fully at the same time.

examples.text: There's a trade-off between taking more modules and doing well in each.
There's always a trade-off between covering the syllabus and going deep.
The trade-off is speed versus consistency; which matters more here?
There's a trade-off between a cheaper flight and a 5 a.m. start.

synonyms.note: An agreement where both sides give something up.
Economics: what you give up by choosing one option.

commonMistake: Noun: 'trade-off' (hyphenated). Verb: 'trade off' (two words), e.g. 'trade off speed for safety'.
origin: From 'trade', to exchange: giving up one thing in exchange for another.

upgrade.plain: We can make it faster, but it'll be less accurate.
upgrade.model: The trade-off is between speed and accuracy.

definition: Able to grow or handle more demand without failing or losing efficiency.

examples.text: The mentoring scheme worked for one class, but it isn't scalable to the whole year.
Marking every book every night isn't scalable; we need a smarter feedback approach.
Is the current architecture scalable to ten times the traffic?
Hosting Christmas for twenty isn't scalable in our tiny kitchen.

synonyms.note: Can be made bigger; less about performance.
Can continue over time without exhaustion.

origin: From 'scale', in the sense of size or extent.

upgrade.plain: This process won't work if we have many more customers.
upgrade.model: This process isn't scalable.

definition: Strong and unlikely to fail; able to cope with difficult conditions.

examples.text: Your conclusions need more robust evidence.
We need a robust system for tracking homework that doesn't rely on memory.
The parser needs to be robust to malformed input.
We need a more robust umbrella for this weather.

synonyms.note: Recovers from problems, rather than resisting them.
Consistently works; less about tough conditions.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of a debate or response: forceful, even heated (a British euphemism).
otherMeanings.example: The minister faced some robust questioning on the radio this morning.
otherMeanings.cue: 'A robust exchange of views' usually means a row.

origin: Latin 'robustus', firm and hard, from 'robur', oak.

upgrade.plain: We need a stronger process that won't break easily.
upgrade.model: We need a more robust process.

definition: Very detailed; broken down into small parts.

examples.text: The feedback was granular, with comments on almost every paragraph.
Question-level analysis gives a granular picture of which topics need reteaching.
We need more granular permissions; 'admin' or 'viewer' isn't enough.
My mum wants a granular account of our holiday, down to every meal.

synonyms.note: Thorough; about depth rather than small parts.

origin: Latin 'granulum', small grain.

upgrade.plain: Can you give me a more detailed breakdown of the costs?
upgrade.model: Can you give me a more granular breakdown of the costs?

definition: To use something you have to its full advantage.

examples.text: Leverage your placement experience in your personal statement.
We can leverage the science club's enthusiasm for the open evening.
We can leverage the existing auth service instead of building our own.
We leveraged our loyalty points to get free cinema tickets.

synonyms.note: Use as a foundation for more.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun) Power or influence you can use to get what you want.
otherMeanings.example: As their biggest client, we've got some leverage in the negotiations.

commonMistake: Overused in business speak. Ask yourself whether 'use' would do; often it would. British pronunciation: 'LEE-ver-idge'.
origin: From 'lever', a bar that lets a small force move a heavy weight.

upgrade.plain: We should use the data we already have.
upgrade.model: We should leverage the data we already have.

definition: To agree on, or bring into agreement, goals or plans.

examples.text: Let's align on the structure before we each write our sections.
Our department's marking needs to align with the exam board's criteria.
Can we align on the API contract before both teams start building?
Let's align on dates before we book the cottage.

synonyms.note: Organise so that things work together.

origin: French 'à ligne', into line.

upgrade.plain: Let's agree on the priorities before Monday.
upgrade.model: Let's align on the priorities before Monday.

definition: To decide the order of importance of tasks and deal with the most important first.

examples.text: With three deadlines in one week, I had to prioritise ruthlessly.
Prioritise the topics that carry the most marks in the exam.
We'll prioritise the security fix over the new feature.
This weekend I'm prioritising sleep over the garden.

synonyms.note: Sort by urgency, from medicine; common in support teams.

commonMistake: British spelling: 'prioritise'; 'prioritize' is American.
origin: Latin 'prior', first.

upgrade.plain: We should deal with the urgent bugs first.
upgrade.model: We should prioritise the urgent bugs.

definition: To pass a problem to someone more senior; also, to become more serious.

examples.text: If the landlord doesn't reply, I'll escalate it to the accommodation office.
If the behaviour continues, I'll escalate it to the head of year.
If it isn't fixed in an hour, escalate to the on-call manager.
If the landlord ignores the leak, escalate it to the council.

synonyms.note: Pass to someone else; no sense of seniority.

origin: From 'escalator': moving up a level.

upgrade.plain: If we can't solve it, we'll pass it up to the manager.
upgrade.model: If we can't resolve it, we'll escalate it to the manager.

definition: Something that stops work from progressing until it is resolved.

examples.text: Our main blocker is waiting for ethics approval.
The blocker for the trip is getting enough staff to supervise.
Any blockers? I'm waiting on access to the staging database.
The main blocker to moving house is selling our flat.

synonyms.note: Slows things down rather than stopping them.
Something you're waiting on from someone else.

origin: From 'block', to obstruct.

upgrade.plain: I can't continue until I get the login details.
upgrade.model: My blocker is getting the login details.

definition: The gradual, uncontrolled growth of a project's requirements beyond what was agreed.

examples.text: Our dissertation suffered from scope creep; we tried to answer three questions instead of one.
The school trip has had serious scope creep: it's now a three-day residential.
Let's park that idea; it's scope creep for this release.
Our 'quick' kitchen refresh has suffered serious scope creep.

synonyms.note: Software-specific: more and more features added.

origin: 'Scope' (the agreed extent) plus 'creep' (moving slowly and unnoticed).

upgrade.plain: The project keeps getting bigger because people keep adding things.
upgrade.model: The project is suffering from scope creep.

definition: An unusual situation at the extreme limits of normal operation.

examples.text: The policy works for most students, but part-time learners are an edge case.
Zero is an edge case: is it even, odd, or neither? Let's discuss.
What happens in the edge case where the list is empty?
What about the edge case where it rains on the day of the barbecue?

synonyms.note: Where two or more edge conditions combine.
Data: a value far from the rest.

origin: From the idea of the edge of the range of possible inputs.

upgrade.plain: What if the user has no internet? That's a rare situation we haven't thought about.
upgrade.model: What if the user has no internet? That's an edge case we haven't covered.

definition: The future cost of choosing a quick solution now instead of a better one.

examples.text: Copying the same formula into every cell created technical debt in our spreadsheet.
Skipping the basics creates a kind of technical debt that catches up with pupils in Year 10.
We'll take on some technical debt to hit the deadline, then pay it down next sprint.
Our house has years of technical debt: every previous owner did quick DIY fixes.

synonyms.note: Old code, often with lots of tech debt.

origin: Coined by Ward Cunningham in 1992: like financial debt, it accrues interest.

upgrade.plain: This quick fix will cause problems we'll need to sort out later.
upgrade.model: This quick fix adds technical debt.

definition: Formal approval that allows something to go ahead (verb: 'sign off on').

examples.text: I need my supervisor's sign-off before I start data collection.
The trip needs sign-off from the head before we can tell parents.
We're waiting on sign-off from legal before releasing the new terms.
The extension is still waiting for sign-off from the council.

otherMeanings.meaning: The closing words of an email or letter, such as 'Best wishes'.
otherMeanings.example: 'Cheers' is a friendly sign-off, but too casual for a complaint letter.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Signed off' (sick): when a doctor certifies you're not fit for work.
otherMeanings.example: He's been signed off for two weeks with his back.
otherMeanings.cue: British usage: 'signed off work', 'signed off sick'.

commonMistake: Noun: 'sign-off' (hyphenated). Verb: 'sign off' or 'sign off on'.
origin: From signing your name to approve a document.

upgrade.plain: We need the manager to approve this first.
upgrade.model: We need sign-off from the manager first.

definition: A specific product or result that must be completed as part of a project.

examples.text: The project has three deliverables: a report, a poster and a presentation.
The deliverable for this INSET is a shared scheme of work.
The first deliverable is a working prototype by the end of March.
For the wedding planning, our first deliverable is the guest list.

synonyms.note: A point in time, rather than a product.

origin: From 'deliver', plus '-able'.

upgrade.plain: What do we need to hand in at the end?
upgrade.model: What are the deliverables?

definition: To make a process simpler and more efficient.

examples.text: The new form streamlines the process of applying for extensions.
We've streamlined report writing with a comment bank.
We streamlined the deploy pipeline from forty minutes to eight.
Online booking has really streamlined getting a GP appointment.

synonyms.note: Make as efficient as possible; more technical.
British business: reorganise to cut waste, sometimes cut jobs.

origin: From the shape of an object designed to move smoothly through water or air.

upgrade.plain: The new tool makes ordering simpler and quicker.
upgrade.model: The new tool streamlines ordering.

definition: A return to a worse state; in software, a bug that breaks something that used to work.

examples.text: We ran a linear regression to model the relationship between the variables.
After the holidays there's always some regression in times-table fluency.
This release introduced a regression in the login flow.
After a month off, there's been a noticeable regression in my running.

synonyms.note: General software fault; not necessarily one that broke working code.

otherMeanings.meaning: In statistics, a method for modelling the relationship between variables.
otherMeanings.example: A linear regression showed a strong link between revision hours and scores.
otherMeanings.cue: 'Regression analysis', 'linear regression' and 'regression line' are all statistics.

otherMeanings.meaning: In psychology, slipping back into earlier, more childish behaviour.
otherMeanings.example: Some regression is normal when a toddler gets a new baby brother or sister.

origin: Latin 'regredi', to go back.

upgrade.plain: The update broke something that was working before.
upgrade.model: The update introduced a regression.

definition: The reasons behind a decision or belief.

examples.text: Explain the rationale for choosing interviews over a survey.
Share the rationale with pupils: why are we learning this?
Please add the rationale to the ADR so future readers know why we chose Postgres.
What's the rationale for repainting the hall again?

commonMistake: Pronounced 'rash-uh-NAHL'. Don't confuse with 'rationalise' (to justify, sometimes with false reasons).
origin: Latin 'rationalis', based on reason.

upgrade.plain: Can you explain why you made this decision?
upgrade.model: Can you explain the rationale behind this decision?

definition: General agreement among a group.

examples.text: There's no consensus among historians about the causes of the war.
The department reached a consensus on the new marking policy.
We need consensus from the platform team before changing the shared library.
There's no consensus in our house about pineapple on pizza.

synonyms.note: Informal business term: people's support and commitment.

commonMistake: 'General consensus' and 'consensus of opinion' are redundant. Spelt with an 's' in the middle, not 'concensus'.
origin: Latin 'consentire', to feel together.

upgrade.plain: Everyone more or less agrees we should delay.
upgrade.model: There's a broad consensus that we should delay.

definition: A future event that might happen, or a plan for dealing with it.

examples.text: Build in a week of contingency in case the data collection runs late.
Always have a contingency plan in case the computers don't work.
We've added 20% contingency to the estimate for unknowns.
Pack a contingency jumper; it's the Lake District.

synonyms.note: Extra time or money set aside.

origin: Latin 'contingere', to happen or to touch.

upgrade.plain: What's our backup plan if the supplier is late?
upgrade.model: What's our contingency plan if the supplier is late?

definition: To make a process or action easier; to help a discussion run smoothly.

examples.text: I volunteered to facilitate the group's first planning meeting.
My role in the debate is to facilitate, not to give my own opinion.
Can you facilitate the retro this week? I'll take notes.
The new bus route will facilitate getting to the hospital.

commonMistake: People facilitate things, not people: 'facilitate learning', not 'facilitate students'.
origin: Latin 'facilis', easy.

upgrade.plain: I'll run the workshop and keep the discussion going.
upgrade.model: I'll facilitate the workshop.

definition: To give a task or responsibility to someone else.

examples.text: As group leader, I delegated the research to Priya and the slides to Tom.
Delegate the equipment set-up to two reliable pupils.
